courseTitle: PowerShell, Python, Azure CLI & Infrastructure Automation

lessons.title: Why Infrastructure Automation Matters at Scale

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one of the lesson's three scenarios (provisioning 50 VMs, tagging every resource in a subscription for a cost center, or rotating credentials across many storage accounts) and write a one-paragraph breakdown of exactly how that task would fail using only manual console clicks — naming which of the three failure modes (not repeatable, error-prone, not auditable) would bite first and why.
slots.deliverable: A written paragraph naming one of the lesson's three scenarios and the specific failure mode (not repeatable / error-prone / not auditable) that manual console work would hit first.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Tool: PowerShell, Python, or CLI

slots.practicalActivity: For 3 different automation tasks you invent (one clearly Windows/Azure-heavy, one needing cross-platform logic plus a non-cloud library, one that's 'run 5 CLI commands in order on a Linux build server'), write one sentence each naming which of the three tools — PowerShell, Python, or a Bash CLI script — fits best, using the lesson's own criteria (the Az module and Verb-Noun pattern, cross-platform plus the library ecosystem, or no-module-needed portability).
slots.deliverable: 3 written sentences, each naming a tool (PowerShell, Python, or Bash CLI) for a different invented task and citing the lesson's actual reasoning for that choice.

lessons.title: Idempotency: Why a Script Should Be Safe to Rerun

slots.practicalActivity: On a real or trial Azure subscription, take the lesson's 'NOT idempotent' New-AzResourceGroup line and rewrite it using the Get-AzResourceGroup -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue check-then-act pattern from the lesson, then actually run the rewritten version twice in a row to confirm the second run makes no change and throws no error.
slots.deliverable: Working PowerShell using the check-then-act idempotency pattern on a resource group, run twice in a row with no error or duplicate on the second run.

lessons.title: Error Handling in Automation Scripts

slots.practicalActivity: Write a 3-step PowerShell script (resource group, storage account, a third placeholder step) where step 2 is wrapped in try/catch with exit 1 on failure, exactly as the lesson shows. Deliberately break step 2 (e.g. an invalid storage account name) and confirm step 3 never runs and the script exits with a non-zero code you check via $LASTEXITCODE.
slots.deliverable: A 3-step script with try/catch around step 2, proven by a deliberately broken run where step 3 never executes and a non-zero exit code is confirmed.

lessons.title: The Az PowerShell Module in Depth

slots.practicalActivity: Run Get-Module -Name Az.* -ListAvailable | Select-Object Name, Version | Sort-Object Name on your own machine and record which Az sub-modules are actually installed. Then run Get-InstalledModule -Name Az and Update-Module -Name Az to confirm you're on the latest version, and write 2 sentences on which specific sub-modules (Az.Compute, Az.Storage, Az.Resources) a VM-only runbook would actually need imported versus the full Az umbrella.
slots.deliverable: Real Get-Module -Name Az.* output listing your installed sub-modules, plus confirmation Update-Module -Name Az ran, and 2 written sentences on minimal sub-module dependencies for a VM-only script.

lessons.title: Looping Over Azure Resources with PowerShell

slots.practicalActivity: Against your own Azure subscription (or a free trial), run the lesson's Get-AzVM -Status | ForEach-Object { [PSCustomObject]@{...} } | Format-Table power-state report for real. Then tag at least one VM Environment = Dev and run the Where-Object { $_.Tags["Environment"] -eq "Dev" } filtered-stop pattern against it with -NoWait, confirming only the tagged VM was targeted.
slots.deliverable: Real Format-Table output from a Get-AzVM -Status power-state report, plus proof that a tag-filtered Where-Object/ForEach-Object pipeline targeted only the one VM you tagged Environment=Dev.

lessons.title: PowerShell Functions for Reusable Automation

slots.practicalActivity: Write the lesson's Get-StoppedVMs function with its param() block and [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)] attribute, then write a second function, Start-AllStoppedVMs, that calls it, exactly as the lesson builds it. Run Get-StoppedVMs once with the parameter omitted to confirm PowerShell enforces the mandatory parameter, then run it correctly against a real or invented resource group name.
slots.deliverable: Working Get-StoppedVMs and Start-AllStoppedVMs functions (the second calling the first), plus proof that omitting the mandatory -ResourceGroupName parameter is rejected by PowerShell.

lessons.title: Scheduling PowerShell Scripts with Azure Automation

slots.practicalActivity: In a real or sandboxed Azure subscription, create an Automation account with New-AzAutomationAccount, import the Lesson 6 stop-tagged-VMs script as a runbook with Import-AzAutomationRunbook -Type PowerShell, publish it with Publish-AzAutomationRunbook, then create a daily schedule with New-AzAutomationSchedule and link it to the runbook with Register-AzAutomationScheduledRunbook.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure Automation account containing one published runbook (built from Lesson 6's script) linked to a daily schedule via Register-AzAutomationScheduledRunbook.

lessons.title: Why Python for Cloud Automation

slots.practicalActivity: Confirm Python's cross-platform claim yourself: run python --version and a short script that prints a VM-tagging decision on whichever OS you have (Windows, WSL, Mac, or Linux). Then write 2 sentences naming one task from this course so far that would get genuinely harder in PowerShell alone versus Python, and why — citing the lesson's 'official SDK' point.
slots.deliverable: Confirmed Python version output from your own machine, plus 2 written sentences naming one real task that favors Python's cross-platform/official-SDK advantage over PowerShell.

lessons.title: The Azure SDK for Python and Boto3 for AWS

slots.practicalActivity: In a real Python virtual environment, run pip install azure-identity azure-mgmt-compute boto3. Write and run the lesson's compute_client.virtual_machines.list_all() loop against a real or trial Azure subscription (or the s3_resource.buckets.all() loop against a free-tier AWS account), printing each resource's name and a second property.
slots.deliverable: A real Python virtual environment with azure-identity, azure-mgmt-compute, and boto3 installed, plus console output from a working virtual_machines.list_all() or buckets.all() loop run against a real account.

lessons.title: Authenticating Python Scripts to Azure and AWS

slots.practicalActivity: Run az login, then run DefaultAzureCredential() from a Python script on your own machine and confirm in the lesson's own terms that it picked up your locally signed-in session (the chain's third source). Separately, check whether ~/.aws/credentials exists on your machine and write one sentence on which Boto3 credential-chain source would actually be used if this script ran on your laptop versus on an EC2 instance.
slots.deliverable: A working DefaultAzureCredential() script that authenticates via your local az login session, plus one written sentence identifying which Boto3 credential source applies on your laptop versus on EC2.

lessons.title: A Real Python Script to Provision a Resource

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's complete Python script end to end against a real or trial Azure subscription — create a resource group with resource_groups.create_or_update, then a storage account with storage_client.storage_accounts.begin_create(...), calling .result() and printing the created account's name. If you're AWS-only, run the equivalent Boto3 S3 bucket script instead, remembering LocationConstraint for any region other than us-east-1.
slots.deliverable: Console output showing a real storage account (or S3 bucket) created end to end by running the lesson's complete script, including the printed confirmation line.

lessons.title: Writing a Bash Script with the az CLI

slots.practicalActivity: Save the lesson's complete check-tags.sh script exactly as written, chmod +x it, and run it against your own (or a trial) Azure subscription's real resource groups, confirming it correctly reports OK or MISSING for the Environment tag on each one.
slots.deliverable: A real, executable check-tags.sh run against your own Azure subscription, with console output showing at least one OK and ideally one MISSING result against real resource groups.

lessons.title: Writing a Bash Script with the AWS CLI

slots.practicalActivity: Save the lesson's complete check-ec2-owners.sh script, chmod +x it, and run it against a real or free-tier AWS account's EC2 instances (even a single stopped t2.micro). Confirm the None-string quirk yourself by checking an instance with no Owner tag and verifying the script's [ "$OWNER" == "None" ] check — not a -z check — catches it correctly.
slots.deliverable: A real, executable check-ec2-owners.sh run against a real AWS account, with output demonstrating the None-string check correctly flagging an instance with no Owner tag.

lessons.title: Parsing CLI JSON Output with jq

slots.practicalActivity: Install jq and run all 3 of the lesson's real filter patterns against your own cloud's CLI output: the identity filter jq '.' on az vm list --output json (or aws ec2 describe-instances --output json), a select() filter isolating only running instances, and a string-interpolation filter combining two fields into one readable line.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output from 3 working jq filters (identity ., a select() filter, and a string-interpolation filter) run against real az or aws JSON output.

lessons.title: A Script That Reconciles Resources Across Both Clouds

slots.practicalActivity: Save and run the lesson's complete multi-cloud-inventory.sh script against real or trial Azure and AWS accounts, confirming the jq '. | length' Azure VM count, the non-terminated AWS instance count from the select(.State.Name != "terminated") filter, the $(( )) arithmetic total, and the -gt/-eq comparison all produce correct real numbers.
slots.deliverable: Real output from multi-cloud-inventory.sh run against both a real Azure and a real AWS account, showing the VM count, non-terminated instance count, combined total, and the comparison result.

lessons.title: What "Ground Truth" Infrastructure as Code Solves

slots.practicalActivity: On a real resource you've already created in this course, run az deployment group what-if --resource-group <your-rg> --template-file <a minimal Bicep file declaring the same resource> to see real drift-detection output. Then write 2 sentences: one naming a concrete example of configuration drift (someone manually changing a setting in the portal), and one explaining why none of Chapters 1-4's scripts could have detected it on their own.
slots.deliverable: Real az deployment group what-if output run against one of your own resources, plus 2 written sentences on a concrete drift example and why an imperative script can't catch it.

lessons.title: ARM Templates and Bicep: A First Look

slots.practicalActivity: Write a minimal real Bicep file declaring one storage account, following the lesson's exact example, run az bicep build to see the ARM JSON it compiles to, then deploy it with az deployment group create --resource-group <your-rg> --template-file storage.bicep against a real or trial subscription. Run the deployment a second time to confirm nothing changes.
slots.deliverable: A real .bicep file for a storage account, its compiled ARM JSON from az bicep build, and proof of az deployment group create run twice with no change on the second run.

lessons.title: AWS CloudFormation: A First Look

slots.practicalActivity: Write the lesson's exact CloudFormation YAML template declaring one S3 bucket with versioning enabled and public access blocked, deploy it with aws cloudformation deploy --template-file bucket.yaml --stack-name ltv-demo-stack against a real or free-tier AWS account, then run aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift --stack-name ltv-demo-stack.
slots.deliverable: A real deployed CloudFormation stack from the lesson's bucket.yaml template, plus real output from aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift run against it.

lessons.title: Why This Path Goes Deeper on Terraform Next

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-paragraph comparison, in your own words, of why a company running only Azure can reasonably pick Bicep, a company running only AWS can reasonably pick CloudFormation, but a company running both faces a real two-syntax maintenance problem that Terraform's provider model removes — naming the specific concepts (provider, HCL) from the lesson.
slots.deliverable: A written paragraph explaining the Bicep-vs-CloudFormation-vs-Terraform tradeoff for a multi-cloud company, correctly naming "provider" and "HCL."

lessons.title: Automating VM Start/Stop Schedules for Cost Savings

slots.practicalActivity: On a real or trial Azure subscription, tag at least one test VM AutoShutdown = true using Update-AzTag, then run both the lesson's complete stop-tagged-vms.ps1 and start-tagged-vms.ps1 scripts against it, confirming with Get-AzVM -Status that the VM actually deallocates (not just a guest-OS shutdown) and restarts. Calculate yourself the real percentage cost reduction for a 10-hour weekday schedule versus 168 hours/week.
slots.deliverable: Real Get-AzVM -Status output proving a tagged VM was deallocated by stop-tagged-vms.ps1 and restarted by start-tagged-vms.ps1, plus your own calculated percentage cost reduction for a 50-hour week.

lessons.title: Automating Tag Compliance Checks

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's complete check-tag-compliance.ps1 script with $requiredTags = @("CostCenter", "Environment") against your own real or trial subscription, confirming it correctly reports every resource missing one or both tags using the ContainsKey plus null-check logic. Then fix one reported resource with Update-AzTag and rerun the script to confirm it drops off the non-compliant list.
slots.deliverable: Real Format-Table output from check-tag-compliance.ps1 showing at least one non-compliant resource, plus a second run after an Update-AzTag fix showing that resource is no longer listed.

lessons.title: Automating Backup Verification

slots.practicalActivity: If you have an Azure Recovery Services vault (or can create a trial one), run the lesson's complete check-backup-jobs.ps1 script with the real -From (Get-Date).AddHours(-24) -To (Get-Date) rolling window against it. If you don't have a vault, write out the exact script and trace through, in writing, what Where-Object { $_.Status -ne "Completed" } would catch that a filter matching only "Failed" would miss.
slots.deliverable: Either real output from check-backup-jobs.ps1 run against a vault, or a written walkthrough of exactly which backup job statuses the -ne "Completed" filter catches that a -eq "Failed" filter would miss.

lessons.title: Automating a Simple Incident Response Action

slots.practicalActivity: Install the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK and, against a test/sandbox tenant only, never a production account, run Connect-MgGraph with the lesson's two scopes and execute the full contain-compromised-account.ps1 script against one disposable test user — confirming Update-MgUser -AccountEnabled:$false disabled it and Revoke-MgUserSignInSession ran — then write one sentence explaining why the UPN parameter is marked Mandatory rather than defaulted.
slots.deliverable: Real Microsoft Graph output confirming a disposable test account was disabled and had its sessions revoked by the lesson's script, plus one written sentence on why the UPN parameter must be mandatory.

lessons.title: Why Automation Scripts Belong in Source Control

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real Git repository, commit one script from earlier in this course into it, then make a second commit that deliberately introduces the lesson's exact dangerous mistake (remove a -notlike "prod-*"-style safety filter from a cleanup loop), and practice git log --oneline followed by git revert to undo that specific commit.
slots.deliverable: A real Git repo with a script committed, a second commit removing a safety filter, and proof that git revert against that specific commit's hash restored the safer version.

lessons.title: Running a Script from a Pipeline, Not a Laptop

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real GitHub Actions workflow file under .github/workflows/ using the lesson's exact trigger block (schedule: cron plus workflow_dispatch) and runs-on: ubuntu-latest, push it to a real GitHub repo, and manually trigger it once via the workflow_dispatch button to confirm it runs on a hosted runner and produces a logged run you can open afterward.
slots.deliverable: A real GitHub Actions workflow file pushed to a repo, triggered once via workflow_dispatch, with a viewable logged run confirming it executed on a hosted runner.

lessons.title: Secrets in Pipelines: Not Hardcoded, Not in Logs

slots.practicalActivity: In a real GitHub repo, add a fake credential value under Settings -> Secrets and variables -> Actions, reference it in a workflow step as ${{ secrets.YOUR_SECRET_NAME }}, and run the workflow to confirm GitHub masks it in the log. Then add a second step that deliberately echoes a transformed (e.g. base64-encoded) version of the secret and observe whether GitHub's masking still catches it.
slots.deliverable: A real GitHub Actions secret referenced correctly in a workflow with confirmed masking in the run log, plus your own observation of whether a transformed/encoded version of the secret was still masked.

lessons.title: A Real Pipeline That Runs a Provisioning Script

slots.practicalActivity: Write the lesson's complete 4-step GitHub Actions workflow (trigger, actions/checkout@v4, azure/login@v2 with a real or sandboxed service principal stored as a GitHub secret, then a run step calling one of your own PowerShell scripts from earlier in this course) and trigger it manually to confirm all four steps execute and the script actually runs against Azure from the hosted runner.
slots.deliverable: A real, working GitHub Actions workflow with all 4 steps (trigger, checkout, Azure login via a stored secret, script run) triggered manually with a successful logged run.

lessons.title: Lab: Building a Cost-Savings Automation Script

slots.practicalActivity: Build Thornfield Analytics' complete cost-savings script yourself: the tag-based Where-Object { $_.Tags["AutoShutdown"] -eq "true" } targeting, the power-state check that only acts when $state -eq "VM running", and the try/catch-with-continue wrapper around each VM so one failure doesn't stop the loop. Run it twice in a row against a real or trial subscription's tagged test VM(s) and confirm the second run's output reports "already '...' — nothing to do" instead of attempting the stop again.
slots.deliverable: A complete, working cost-savings script combining tag targeting, a power-state idempotency check, and try/catch-with-continue error handling, run twice against real VM(s) with the second run correctly reporting no action needed.

lessons.title: Lab: Building a Compliance-Checking Script

slots.practicalActivity: Build the complete Python compliance script from the lesson: DefaultAzureCredential authentication, the REQUIRED_TAGS = ["CostCenter", "Owner"] check against client.resources.list(), writing violations to a real tag-violations.csv file, and sys.exit(1 if violations else 0). Run it against a real or trial subscription, then check the exit code to confirm it actually changes based on whether violations were found.
slots.deliverable: A working Python script producing a real tag-violations.csv file against a real subscription, plus confirmed exit-code output (0 or 1) that changes correctly based on whether any violations were found.

lessons.title: Case Study: A Script That Prevented an Outage

slots.practicalActivity: Extend your Lesson 30 script with the lesson's exact additional rule — if tags.get("Tier") == "Critical" and tags.get("DoNotDelete") != "true": — and test it against one resource you tag Tier=Critical with no DoNotDelete tag, confirming it's correctly flagged as a violation. Then write a short paragraph walking through Thornfield's near-miss in your own words, naming which specific Chapter 7 practice (source control, pipeline-not-laptop, or pipeline secrets) made the catch possible.
slots.deliverable: Your extended compliance script correctly flagging a Tier: Critical resource missing DoNotDelete, plus a written paragraph naming the specific Chapter 7 practice that made Thornfield's near-miss catch possible.

lessons.title: Chapter Capstone: Infrastructure Automation Review

slots.practicalActivity: Write your own one-paragraph answer to the lesson's closing question: pick one decision from Lesson 29's cost-savings script (tool choice, the idempotency check, or the try/catch-with-continue pattern) and explain specifically what later lesson or earlier chapter made that decision actually pay off, in your own words, without re-reading the lesson's answer first.
slots.deliverable: A written paragraph naming one specific decision from the capstone's cost-savings script and explaining, in your own words, which earlier or later lesson made it pay off.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can write real, idempotent infrastructure-automation scripts in PowerShell, Python, and Bash — authenticating to both Azure and AWS without ever hardcoding a secret, looping over and filtering real cloud resources, wrapping repeated logic in reusable PowerShell functions, parsing multi-cloud CLI JSON output with jq, and reconciling compute inventory across both clouds in one script. They've previewed declarative Infrastructure as Code with a real Bicep deployment and a real CloudFormation stack and can explain why Terraform goes further for multi-cloud teams, automated four real operational tasks end to end (VM start/stop scheduling for cost savings, tag-compliance checking, backup-job verification, and a tightly scoped incident-response containment action), and shipped two capstone scripts — one in PowerShell, one in Python, each idempotent and error-handled — through a real Git repository and a real GitHub Actions pipeline with properly stored secrets, finishing with a concrete, worked example of exactly how that kind of pipeline run catches a dangerous manual mistake before it becomes an outage.
